roots.label: PIE · to snow
roots.description: English snow, Latin nix and the Baltic, Slavic and Goidelic words descend from formations of this reconstructed root. An asterisk marks an unattested reconstruction; spellings vary between reference works.

roots.label: PIE · snow / winter
roots.description: Greek and Armenian preserve a different Indo-European snow/winter word, distinct from *sneygʷʰ-.

roots.label: Brythonic · snow
roots.description: Welsh, Breton and Cornish share this Brythonic word. Its deeper origin is disputed; proposed connections to 'white' or 'scatter' are not treated as established.

roots.label: Slavic · fall
roots.description: Romanian zăpadă is a back-formation from a verb borrowed from Old Church Slavonic 'to fall'; it is not a reflex of the PIE snow root.

roots.label: Albanian · falling
roots.description: Albanian borë comes from a prefixed derivative of the verb 'fall'. The exact Proto-Albanian reconstruction has variants.

roots.label: Iranian · snow
roots.description: Persian barf and Northern Kurdish berf continue Iranian *wafrah, traced to Indo-Iranian *wapras. A deeper PIE connection is not asserted here.

roots.label: Ossetian · snow
roots.description: The word is attested; its deeper history is not established in this atlas. This color indicates a separate unresolved set, not a proposed proto-language.

roots.label: Uralic · snow
roots.description: Finnic lumi and the Mari and Udmurt forms continue the Uralic *lome set.

roots.label: Uralic · snow
roots.description: Hungarian hó belongs to the *kume set. It is a different Uralic snow word from Finnish lumi.

roots.label: Sámi · snow
roots.description: Northern Sámi muohta continues Proto-Sámi *muottëk. The atlas stops at this reconstruction and does not link it to Finnic lumi.

roots.label: Semitic · snow
roots.description: Arabic, Hebrew and Maltese show the Semitic snow set. Maltese silġ also means ice and hail.

roots.label: Turkic · snow
roots.description: Turkish kar, Kazakh қар and their relatives continue a Proto-Turkic snow word. No Indo-European relationship is asserted.

roots.label: Kartvelian · snow
roots.description: Georgian თოვლი continues a Kartvelian snow stem. The chain is independent of the Indo-European snow root.

roots.label: Basque · snow
roots.description: Basque elur continues reconstructed Proto-Basque *eruR. R is a conventional reconstruction symbol. No Indo-European connection is asserted.

roots.label: Berber · snow
roots.description: Related snow words occur in several Berber languages. These are modern forms; no exact Proto-Berber form is reconstructed here.

roots.label: Nakh · snow
roots.description: Chechen ло continues a Nakh snow word. No relationship with the other displayed sets is asserted.

roots.label: Norse: snowdrift / submerge
roots.description: Faroese kavi has a separate Norse history from the poetic snjógvur. Its precise derivation is uncertain; the cited lexical source connects it with kaf (snowdrift / submersion) or kafa (submerge). A deeper proto-root is not asserted.

roots.label: Samoyedic
roots.description: Tundra Nenets сыра continues Proto-Samoyedic *sïrå. This noun is kept separate from the *lome set; sharing the Uralic family does not establish the same lexical root.

roots.label: Avar
roots.description: The attested Avar snow word. No deeper reconstruction or relationship to the other Caucasian sets is asserted here.

sources.title: Avar Dictionary, Universitat Pompeu Fabra: гӀазу

roots.label: Dargwa
roots.description: The Dargwa citation form in the comparative word list. Dargwa comprises many varieties; no deeper reconstruction is asserted here.

roots.label: Lezgian
roots.description: The attested Lezgian snow word. The comparative list and Russian lemma give жив; the English Wiktionary translation table also has жиз. This atlas uses жив and does not infer a deeper ancestor.

roots.label: Lak
roots.description: The attested Lak word in the Russian–Lak dictionary. No deeper reconstruction is asserted here.

sources.title: Russian–Lak dictionary, Dagestan State University: снег / марххала, p. 327

roots.label: Circassian
roots.description: The East and West Circassian words are compared in their lexical entries. They form a local comparative set here; no exact Proto-Circassian form or wider Caucasian relationship is asserted.

roots.label: Mongolic
roots.description: Kalmyk цасн continues Proto-Mongolic *časun, also reflected by Mongolian цас. No connection with Turkic *kār is asserted.

roots.label: Greenlandic
roots.description: The attested Greenlandic snow word. Oqaasileriffik describes it as the general term for snow on the ground. This set does not assert a deeper reconstruction.

sources.title: Greenlandic–English Dictionary (University of Chicago and Oqaasileriffik, 2018): aput
Oqaasileriffik, Language Secretariat of Greenland: terms for snow and ice

languages.name: Norwegian
languages.notes: The displayed form is shared by modern Bokmål and Nynorsk; the atlas does not divide these writing standards.

languages.name: Faroese
languages.notes: Kavi is the unmarked snow noun used here. The poetic / archaic alternative snjógvur belongs to the PIE snow set. Kavi has a separate Norse history: the consulted source connects it with kaf (snowdrift / submersion) or kafa (submerge). The exact derivation is uncertain, so no deeper proto-root is asserted.

languages.name: Occitan
languages.notes: Regional variants include Aranese nhèu, Limousin neu and deverbal neja / nevia.

languages.name: Sardinian
languages.notes: A Nuorese form; other Sardinian forms include Logudorese nie and Campidanese ni / nia.

languages.name: Friulian
languages.notes: Other forms include nêv.

languages.name: Romansh
languages.notes: Regional forms include nev and neif.

languages.name: Asturian
languages.notes: Also nieve / neve; the displayed form does not represent every dialect.

languages.name: French
languages.notes: Neige is a noun formed from the verb neiger; it replaced the inherited noun noif. This is a schematic derivational chain, not a sound-by-sound chronology.

languages.name: Romanian
languages.notes: A back-formation from a Slavic-derived verb. Romanian also has inherited nea, from Latin nix / nivem, which belongs to the PIE snow set.

languages.name: Serbian–Croatian–Bosnian
languages.notes: The single source footprint combines closely related standards. Ijekavian snijeg (снијег), Ekavian sneg (снег), and Ikavian snig vary by dialect; these are not separate country-sized etymologies.

languages.name: Scottish Gaelic
languages.notes: Also sneachda; both forms occur. The displayed shorter form is retained for comparison.

languages.name: Welsh
languages.notes: Deeper origin is uncertain; the map does not force a link with the PIE snow root.

languages.name: Breton
languages.notes: Deeper origin is uncertain; the map does not force a link with the PIE snow root.

languages.name: Cornish
languages.notes: Deeper origin is uncertain; the map does not force a link with the PIE snow root.

languages.name: Armenian
languages.notes: Eastern Armenian spelling and transliteration shown; traditional orthography ձիւն is also used. The source geometry may combine Eastern and Western Armenian varieties, whose pronunciations differ. The poster reading dzyun is explicitly used by the Bararan Armenian dictionary; the full lexical entry retains scholarly jyun.

languages.name: Albanian
languages.notes: Borë is a shortened form of dëborë; further root identification is not asserted.

languages.name: Northern Kurdish
languages.notes: The atlas uses Northern Kurdish (Kurmanji); Kurdish varieties are not identical.

languages.name: Ossetian
languages.notes: Lexical form verified. The consulted entry gives no etymology, so the deeper chain is deliberately left open.

languages.name: Karelian
languages.notes: Karelian varieties have local variation; one dictionary citation form is shown.

languages.name: Hungarian
languages.notes: This is distinct from the Uralic *lome set represented by Finnish lumi.

languages.name: Northern Sámi
languages.notes: This is one general snow word. Sámi has numerous terms for snow conditions; it is not interchangeable with every one of them.

languages.name: Meadow Mari
languages.notes: Eastern / Meadow Mari form shown. If the source geometry combines Mari varieties, Hill Mari лым (lym) differs in form but belongs to the same root set.

languages.name: Basque
languages.notes: Dialectal forms include edur, elhur and erur.

languages.name: Arabic (standard reference)
languages.notes: Modern Standard Arabic reference form. Local Arabic varieties differ; a standard form must not be read as the only vernacular word throughout North Africa.

languages.name: Hebrew
languages.notes: Vowel points are included for reading; ordinary Hebrew generally writes שלג.

languages.name: Maltese
languages.notes: Silġ can mean snow, ice or hail. Borra is another word for snow / sleet, with a separate Sicilian-derived history.

languages.name: Tunisian Arabic
languages.notes: Tunisian citation form; local pronunciation and spelling vary.

languages.name: Egyptian Arabic
languages.notes: Also used for ice; the displayed Egyptian form reflects t- and g- rather than Standard Arabic th- and j-.

languages.name: Syrian Arabic
languages.notes: Selected regional reading: telj. Map romanization supplied by the map author; local pronunciations and spellings vary.

sources.title: Wiktionary: ثلج (Arabic etymology and regional forms)

languages.name: Mesopotamian Arabic
languages.notes: Selected regional reading: thelij. Map romanization supplied by the map author; local pronunciations and spellings vary.

sources.title: Wiktionary: ثلج (Arabic etymology and regional forms)

languages.name: Kabyle
languages.notes: Related to Berber adfl / adfeř forms. No exact Proto-Berber reconstruction is asserted.

languages.name: Central Atlas Tamazight
languages.notes: A Central Atlas Tamazight form, not an assertion that all Berber languages use the same spelling.

languages.name: Tachelhit
languages.notes: Also atfl; Tifinagh ⴰⴷⴼⵍ. Cognate with the Central Atlas Tamazight and Kabyle snow set.

languages.name: Chechen
languages.notes: Vowel length may be indicated as ло̄ in dictionary notation. The poster uses the lemma’s romanization loo to retain this length indication.

languages.name: Turkmen
languages.notes: Standard Turkmen spelling is gar; some comparative sources mark its long vowel as gār.

languages.name: Komi-Zyrian
languages.notes: Komi-Zyrian citation form. Komi-Permyak also has лым, but is a distinct variety.

languages.name: Tundra Nenets
languages.notes: The source also records the winter sense. This entry specifically represents Tundra Nenets; it does not collapse every Nenets variety.

languages.name: Avar
languages.notes: Attested modern word; the deeper lexical history is left unresolved. The first consonant uses Cyrillic palochka Ӏ. The poster reading ghazu is the source dictionary’s explicitly supplied plain-keyboard spelling, alongside its scholarly ʕazu.

sources.title: Avar Dictionary, Universitat Pompeu Fabra: гӀазу

languages.name: Dargwa
languages.notes: Representative citation form from the comparative list. Dargwa varieties have substantial lexical and phonological variation. The scholarly romanization dəḥi follows the checked Dargwa transliteration table (я → ə, хӏ → ḥ); it is a reading aid rather than an English phonetic respelling. No deeper reconstruction is asserted.

sources.title: Institute of the Estonian Language: Transliteration of Dargwa, TITUS column

languages.name: Lezgian
languages.notes: The Russian Wiktionary lemma and the comparative Swadesh list agree on жив. The English translation table instead lists жиз; that conflicting spelling is not silently treated as a separate ancestry claim.

languages.name: Lak
languages.notes: Checked in the Russian–Lak dictionary at p. 327. Romanization markhkhala follows the checked ALA-LC column of the Lak transliteration table (хх → khkh); the doubled consonant is retained. No deeper root is asserted.

sources.title: Russian–Lak dictionary, Dagestan State University: снег / марххала, p. 327
Institute of the Estonian Language: Transliteration of Lak, ALA-LC column

languages.name: Ingush
languages.notes: The noun is recorded as loa in the UC Berkeley Ingush word list. Comparative reconstructions also use *lawe or *law(a).

sources.title: Johanna Nichols, UC Berkeley: Ingush Swadesh word list

languages.name: Kabardian
languages.notes: The lemma citation form is уэс; inflected or indefinite forms can include a final э. The comparison with West Circassian is sourced, but an exact proto-form is not asserted.

languages.name: Adyghe
languages.notes: West Circassian citation form. The source also gives Shapsug ос (wos).

languages.name: Karachay-Balkar
languages.notes: The mapping unit combines Karachay and Balkar; the cited standard snow word is shared.

languages.name: Kalmyk
languages.notes: Kalmyk citation form, used for the European Kalmyk portion of the broader Oirad-Kalmyk-Darkhat source unit.

languages.name: Balochi
languages.notes: Balochi citation form, also written برف (barf). Balochi includes several varieties; this is a reference word rather than a claim of uniform pronunciation across all source areas.

languages.name: Northern Luri
languages.notes: The reconstruction source groups this modern form with Iranian *wafrah and lists it under Middle Persian descendants. The map records the lexical set; the precise balance of inheritance and contact with Persian is not independently established for each Luri variety.

languages.name: Southern Luri
languages.notes: The reconstruction source groups this modern form with Iranian *wafrah and lists it under Middle Persian descendants. The map records the lexical set; the precise balance of inheritance and contact with Persian is not independently established for each Luri variety.

languages.name: Bakhtiari
languages.notes: The modern word and its Iranian lexical grouping are recorded in the comparative reconstruction source. This schematic chain leaves Persian contact versus direct inheritance unresolved.

languages.name: Central Kurdish
languages.notes: Central Kurdish / Sorani citation form. The lemma transliterates it befr; comparative sources can use bafr. The source also records وەفر (wefr).

languages.name: Greenlandic
languages.notes: Standard Greenlandic reference word, used for the clipped Greenland land fragment. The official snow terminology distinguishes snow on the ground (aput) from snow falling in the air (qaniit); this map uses the general noun aput. It does not claim that Greenland is dialectally uniform.

methodology.title: Lexical and etymological method
methodology.scope: 99 selected language entries for Europe and its surrounding regions. Each entry gives a representative noun meaning snow; the selection is not an exhaustive inventory of every dialect, snow condition or synonym.
methodology.comparison: Colors encode etymological word sets using root, not national borders or general language families. Family and branch remain separate metadata. Membership in Indo-European does not make every word for snow a descendant of *sneygʷʰ-.
methodology.chains: Chains are schematic selections of attested or reconstructed stages, not complete sound histories, exact dates, or claims that all forms coexisted. Intermediate stages may be omitted. Asterisked forms are reconstructed and unattested. Arrows include derivation and, where stated, borrowing; they do not always mean direct inheritance.
methodology.uncertainty: Reconstruction spelling varies by source. The Brythonic deeper origin, Ossetian deeper chain and exact Proto-Berber snow form are deliberately left unresolved. A modern word used as a root label marks a comparative set, not a newly invented proto-form. Faroese kavi is shown separately from poetic / archaic snjógvur, whose PIE snow etymology is retained as an alternative. Avar, Dargwa, Lak and Lezgian are separate attested word sets without a claimed common deep ancestor. Circassian is shown as a local comparison without an invented proto-form. Luri and Bakhtiari membership in the Iranian snow set does not resolve direct inheritance versus Persian contact.
methodology.standards: Some ISO entries are macrolanguages or combined mapping units. A citation form may belong to one variety; notes state material variation. Orthography and romanization are reading aids, not a substitute for IPA. Arabic, Hebrew, Georgian, Armenian and Cyrillic scripts are retained. On the poster, parentheses under non-Latin words give a single romanized reading aid; these are transliterations, not IPA or English phonetic respellings. Scholarly Latin letters and diacritics (for example ə, ɛ, ḥ and ž) are retained where used by the checked source. Arabic th and Hebrew sh are reader-friendly equivalents of scholarly ṯ and š. Dargwa follows the checked Gippert / TITUS table; Lak follows ALA-LC; Avar ghazu is the source dictionary’s plain-keyboard spelling. The mixed Serbo-Croatian label retains both snijeg and sneg rather than implying one uniform pronunciation.
methodology.sources: Lexical entries are primarily cross-checked against Wiktionary lemma and reconstruction pages, which in turn cite dictionaries and etymological reference works. These are accessible secondary lexical sources, not independent fieldwork or a peer-reviewed atlas. Kabyle uses an online Dallet dictionary transcription. Every entry links its lexical source; root descriptions link supporting reconstruction sources. Ambiguous or missing etymologies are not filled by visual similarity. Spanish nieve was additionally checked directly in the RAE dictionary, Catalan neu in the IEC Catalan-Valencian-Balearic dictionary, and Basque elur in an Euskaltzaindia dictionary PDF.
